title: Ordering
subtitle: Preserving causal sequence guarantees from producer retries through partition logs to multi-threaded consumers.
keyTakeaways: Kafka guarantees strict message ordering only within a single partition; there is no global ordering across multiple partitions.
Producer retries without idempotence can corrupt ordering: if Batch 1 times out and Batch 2 succeeds, a successful retry of Batch 1 inverts the message sequence.
In multi-threaded consumers, naively offloading messages to a generic worker thread pool breaks partition ordering; messages must be sharded by entity ID across worker threads.
architectureDiagram:
PRODUCER RETRY OUT-OF-ORDER INVERSION
WITHOUT IDEMPOTENCE (max.in.flight.requests > 1):
Batch 1 (Events 1-100)  ---> Network Timeout / Retried later!
Batch 2 (Events 101-200)---> SUCCEEDS at Broker (Stored at Offset 0-99)
Batch 1 Retry -----------> SUCCEEDS at Broker (Stored at Offset 100-199) -> ORDER INVERTED!

WITH ENABLE.IDEMPOTENCE = TRUE:
Broker tracks Producer ID (PID) + Monotonic Sequence Numbers.
Broker rejects out-of-order batches until Batch 1 completes, preserving strict ordering!

sections.heading: Partition-Level Ordering and Idempotent Producers
sections.body: Preserving causal ordering is essential for state machines. If a user emits `OrderCreated` followed by `OrderCancelled`, processing `OrderCancelled` first results in invalid state transitions.
bullets: The In-Flight Retry Inversion Bug: To maximize throughput, producers send multiple batches in flight concurrently (`max.in.flight.requests.per.connection = 5`). If Batch 1 fails transiently and Batch 2 succeeds, the producer's retry of Batch 1 will be appended after Batch 2 on the broker, corrupting sequence.

Idempotent Producers (`enable.idempotence = true`): Enabled by default in modern Kafka. The broker assigns each producer a unique ID and tracks per-partition monotonic sequence numbers. The broker will not commit Batch 2 until Batch 1 arrives, completely eliminating retry ordering inversions without reducing in-flight pipeline concurrency.

codeSnippet.title: Multi-Threaded Consumer Preserving Entity-Level Ordering

sections.heading: Preserving Ordering on the Consumer Side
sections.body: A frequent architectural blunder occurs when scaling consumer throughput. To speed up processing, a developer pulls a batch of 500 messages from Kafka and throws them into a thread pool (`Promise.all` or Java `ExecutorService`).
bullets: Thread Race Conditions: If the batch contains `UserUpdated(v1)` and `UserUpdated(v2)`, Worker Thread A might take 20ms to process v1 while Worker Thread B processes v2 in 2ms. v2 commits to the database, followed by v1 overwriting it with stale data.

Thread Partitioning by Entity ID: In-process worker thread pools must hash messages by entity ID (`hash(userId) % threadCount`) so that all events for a given entity are processed sequentially by the exact same worker thread.

tradeOffs.pros: Guarantees 100% causal sequence; simple mental model for event processing.
tradeOffs.cons: Throughput bounded by single-partition disk limits (~50 MB/s); can only be consumed by a single worker thread.
tradeOffs.bestFor: Financial trading book matching, bank account ledgers, and inventory reservations.

tradeOffs.pros: Scales horizontally across dozens of partitions; guarantees strict per-entity causal ordering.
tradeOffs.cons: No cross-entity ordering guarantees; vulnerable to partition skew if an individual entity becomes hot.
tradeOffs.bestFor: E-commerce order processing, user activity streams, and messaging chats.

interviewTip: When asked how to scale a slow Kafka consumer with multiple threads without breaking ordering: 'Never dispatch messages from a partition to a random thread pool. To scale processing while preserving ordering, hash each message by entity ID to a dedicated in-memory worker queue, ensuring all events for that specific entity execute sequentially.'
